questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}$ at the point $(0,0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(0,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,0) & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(0+0)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0+0)=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,0) & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(0+0)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0+0)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-1 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,0)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,0) \\ z-1 & =1(x-0)+1(y-0) \\ z-1 & =x+y \\ -x-y+z-1 & =0 \\ x+y-z+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z$ at the point $(2,-2,1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=2{y}^{2}-6xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=4xy+{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=2yz-3{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,-2,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,-2,1) & =2(-2)^{2}-6(2)(1)=-4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,-2,1) & =4(2)(-2)+(1)^{2}=-15 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,-2,1) & =2(-2)(1)-3(2)^{2}=-16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,-2,1)+(y+2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,-2,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,-2,1) \\ w-2 & =-4(x-2)-15(y+2)-16(z-1) \\ w-2 & =-4x+8-15y-30-16z+16 \\ 4x+15y+16z+w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=x+y-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0,1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y-{z}^{2})=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y-{z}^{2})=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+y-{z}^{2})=-2z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,0,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,1) & =1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,1) & =1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,1) & =-2(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,1)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,1) \\ w & =(x-1)+y-2(z-1) \\ w & =x+y-2z+1 \\ x+y-2z-w+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: At which point on the surface $z={x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-7$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $v=⟨6,-8,-1⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-7)=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-7)=4y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x,\,4y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨6,-8,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2x,\,4y,\,-1⟩=⟨6,-8,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2cx=6 \\ 4cy=-8 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2(1)x=6\,⟹\,x=3.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
4(1)y=-8\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=3$ and $y=-2$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & ={3}^{2}+2(-2)^{2}-7 \\  & =9+8-7 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(3,-2,10).$

questions.problem: At which point on the surface $z=4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $v=⟨-2,-5,1⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-4x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-10y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,-5,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4-2{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-5{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4}).$
